beats.intro: Lesson twenty-two. [[sub]]How to feed the drive to achieve, and why work should feel like a sport.
beats.drives: Self-actualization comes in two forms. [[comp]]Some people are competence-driven: they want mastery. [[violin]]A virtuoso violinist practises daily to play a bit better than last time. [[skate]]So does a teenager repeating one skateboard trick. He won't sit ten minutes for homework, but on the board he is relentless. [[ach]]Others are achievement-driven: a need to achieve in everything. [[few]]Not most people, but some.
beats.rings: An experiment showed it. [[room]]Volunteers got rings, a floor with pegs, and no instructions. [[gamb]]Some tossed from far away. High risk, no real control. Gamblers. [[cons]]Some stood over a peg and dropped the ring on. Conservatives. [[achv]]Some stood just far enough away to make it a challenge. Achievers. [[miss]]They missed at first, then ringed the peg steadily, and felt real satisfaction. [[edge]]They work at the edge of what they can do.
beats.fifty: When people don't stretch on their own, the manager builds the environment for it. [[mbo]]With objectives, set each one high enough [[half]]that even a hard push gives only a fifty-fifty chance. [[more]]Output is greater when everyone reaches beyond their grasp, even missing half the time.
beats.output: The environment must also value output. [[lab]]Grove's first job was at a research lab of motivated people, driven to know more, not to produce results. [[little]]Little got done. [[intel]]Intel was the reverse. [[phd]]A Ph.D. who knows the answer but never applies it gets little recognition. [[junior]]A junior engineer who delivers results is esteemed. As it should be.
beats.money: What about money? [[need]]Lower down the ladder, money buys necessities. Once people have what they expect, more won't motivate. [[carib]]At Intel's Caribbean assembly plant, pay was well above the local standard, yet early on many people saved a set sum, then quit. [[vc]]Now take a venture capitalist with ten million dollars, working just as hard for ten million more. [[measure]]Here money is a measure of achievement, and that drive has no limit.
beats.raise: That gives a simple test. [[abs]]If what matters is the size of a raise in dollars, the person is working on the lower needs. [[rel]]If what matters is how it compares with what others got, money is a measure. They are in esteem or self-actualization.
beats.feedback: People in that top mode need measures of progress. [[fb]]Above all, feedback on their performance. [[inner]]For the competence-driven, it is inside. The violinist knows how the music should sound. [[nofb]]But with no room to improve, the drive vanishes. [[fence]]A Hungarian Olympic fencing champion moved to the United States and quit. No one could give him a contest, and every bout made him feel his skill slipping.
beats.relevant: At work, the best measures tie a person's performance to the organization's, [[ind]]like the indicators and milestones in an objectives system. [[irr]]Steer people away from irrelevant rewards, like office size or decor, [[rel]]toward ones that matter. [[review]]The most important task-relevant feedback is the performance review, which comes in a later lesson.
beats.failfear: Fear still plays a part at the top, as fear of failure. [[spur]]On one task, it can spur someone on. [[pre]]As a constant preoccupation, it makes an achiever play safe. [[shock]]Give the ring tossers an electric shock for every miss, and soon they would drop the ring from right above the peg. [[inner]]Up here, the fear comes from within. You can't stay at your personal best if you always worry about failing.
beats.sport: So the manager has two jobs. [[train]]Train people, moving them along the capability axis. [[self]]Then bring them to self-actualization, where motivation sustains itself. [[how]]How? Ask why someone bored at the office runs a marathon. [[beat]]To beat other runners, or the stopwatch. Not for money. [[frazier]]The boxer Joe Frazier was puzzled to be asked why he fought. It was his job, he said, what he was. Money mattered, but not most.
beats.prejudice: Imagine all work with the pull of a competitive sport. [[prej]]First, a prejudice: throwing yourself into sport is admired, but long work hours make you a workaholic. [[join]]So, if you can't beat them, join them. [[rules]]Give work rules of the game, and ways for people to measure themselves. [[against]]Peak performance means going up against something, or somebody.
beats.czar: Grove's example. [[maint]]For years, Intel's building maintenance was mediocre, whatever pressure was tried. [[czar]]Then each building got a building czar, a senior manager who scored its upkeep. [[compare]]Scores were compared across buildings. [[jump]]Every building improved, almost at once. [[nothing]]No money, no rewards. Just a racetrack. [[see]]See the work as the people doing it see it, then create indicators so they can watch their racetrack take shape.
beats.merger: Take the competition away, and that motivation vanishes. [[col]]A newspaper columnist loved beating the rival paper. When the papers merged, he thought: there is no one left to beat. [[lose]]Sport also teaches us to cope with failure. [[half]]In any competitive sport, at least half of all matches are lost. Everyone knows it, [[keep]]and they rarely give up mid-game.
beats.coach: So the manager's role is the coach. [[credit]]A good coach takes no personal credit for the team's success, so the players trust him. [[tough]]He is tough, even critical, to get their best. [[player]]And he was likely a good player once, so he understands the game. [[field]]Make the workplace a playing field, and your people become athletes, performing at their limit.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]Achievers work at the edge of their ability. [[w2]]Set objectives with a fifty-fifty chance, and value output. [[w3]]Money as a need runs out; as a measure, it doesn't. [[w4]]Give task-relevant feedback, and don't punish every miss. [[w5]]Give work a racetrack, and be the coach. Now the lesson practice.

beats.finish: Well done. That is the end of lesson twenty-two, and of part five, on control and motivation.
